title: U.S. Net Zero, Everything Else Unchanged
prompt: Take the CMIP7 Medium and High worlds and construct the temperature path if U.S. net emissions go to zero on a specified schedule while everyone else's development path stays unchanged. Separate official model output from your counterfactual calculation.

title: Who Actually Moves Global Temperature?
prompt: Repeat the same net-zero counterfactual for China, India, the EU, and combinations of them, then put the marginal temperature effects on one common scale.

title: Climate Sensitivity Surgery
prompt: Hold one emissions pathway fixed and rerun the future under several ECS values. Show how much the 2100 outcome is being driven by this single uncertain parameter.

title: Where Does ECS Actually Come From?
prompt: Reconstruct the evidence stack used to constrain equilibrium climate sensitivity and show how an assessed distribution is produced rather than treating one number as directly observed.

title: Cloud Feedback and the Upper Tail
prompt: Use the literature to quantify how alternative cloud-feedback assumptions affect high-end climate sensitivity and resulting temperature distributions.

title: Aerosol Masking
prompt: Start with current estimates of greenhouse warming and anthropogenic aerosol cooling. Change the aerosol term while holding greenhouse gases fixed and show the temperature consequence.

title: The Carbon-Budget Machine
prompt: Start with a published remaining carbon budget. Change probability thresholds, non-CO2 assumptions, starting year, climate sensitivity, or Earth-system feedback assumptions one at a time.

title: What Does One Billion Tons of CO2 Do?
prompt: Use TCRE or a simple climate emulator to translate 1 GtCO2, 10 GtCO2, 100 GtCO2, and one current year of global emissions into expected temperature increments.

title: How Much Does the Terminal Year Matter?
prompt: Take one climate policy and measure modeled benefits and costs through several endpoints such as 2050, 2100, 2200, and 2300.

title: Climate Damages Without Percentage Fog
prompt: Take a published percentage-of-GDP damage estimate and reconstruct two actual future economies—with and without the damage—including GDP per person and aggregate output.

title: Growth Versus Climate Damages
prompt: Hold a climate damage function fixed but change baseline economic growth by small amounts. Compare that effect with changing the climate-damage estimate.

title: Discount-Rate Surgery on the SCC
prompt: Reproduce a social-cost-of-carbon calculation under several discount rates and horizons, then vary growth, climate sensitivity, or damage curvature to see what drives the result.

title: Why SCC Estimates Disagree
prompt: Take several major published SCC estimates and reverse-engineer how much disagreement comes from the climate module, socioeconomic path, damages, mortality, discounting, and tail risk.

title: Heat Deaths, Cold Deaths, and Adaptation
prompt: Use a published mortality-response model under a warming scenario and vary adaptation assumptions. Show heat deaths added, cold deaths avoided, and the net.

title: Same Heat, Different Society
prompt: Apply comparable temperature shocks to populations with different income, air conditioning, demographics, and baseline mortality. Show why temperature alone is not a damage function.

title: Sea-Level Rise: From Centimeters to Risk
prompt: Take several sea-level increments and combine them with real coastal elevation and flood-frequency data. Separate water level, exposure, and expected damage.

title: LCOE Versus an Electricity System
prompt: Build a small power system from actual hourly load. First compare technologies by LCOE; then require demand to be met every hour and show what changes.

title: 100% Renewable for One Real Week
prompt: Take an actual NYISO, PJM, ERCOT, or similar week. Scale wind and solar, identify every surplus and deficit hour, then add storage, overbuild, firm generation, or transmission until the system balances.

title: Four-Hour Batteries Meet a Three-Day Lull
prompt: Use real load and weather data to show what four-hour batteries can solve and what happens during a multi-day wind/solar deficit.

title: Storage-Cost Surgery
prompt: Take a deeply renewable grid and rerun it at several battery costs. Show where storage quantity or system architecture changes.

title: Transmission as a Substitute for Storage
prompt: Connect progressively more weather-diverse regions and quantify how interregional transmission changes storage and overbuild requirements.

title: Firming Wind and Solar
prompt: Construct the cost of delivering one guaranteed MW every hour using wind/solar plus storage, overbuilding, transmission, and dispatchable backup. Compare with raw generation cost.

title: Data Centers: Quantity Constraint or Price Response?
prompt: Take projected data-center load growth in one region. Compare a fixed-supply world with one allowing new generation, transmission, higher prices, load shifting, and delayed projects.

title: How Extraordinary Is Current Electricity-Demand Growth?
prompt: Put current forecasts beside earlier high-growth episodes only to provide scale, then compare how quickly supply expanded then with what is proposed now.

title: Electrify All Passenger Cars
prompt: Calculate added annual electricity, peak load under naive charging, and peak load under managed charging. Put all three beside present generation and peak demand.

title: Electrify Heating
prompt: Model widespread heat-pump adoption in a cold region, including annual energy and winter peak effects under alternative building and equipment assumptions.

title: The Primary-Energy Illusion
prompt: Follow primary energy to useful energy for combustion and electrified alternatives and show why electrification can raise electricity use while reducing total primary energy.

title: Close a Nuclear Plant—What Replaces It?
prompt: Build several replacement cases for one operating nuclear plant and calculate emissions, capacity, land, and cost consequences.

title: New Nuclear Financing
prompt: Hold reactor engineering cost fixed and change construction time and cost of capital. Show how financing alone transforms delivered electricity cost.

title: One Gigawatt Is Not One Gigawatt
prompt: Compare 1-GW nuclear, gas, solar, and wind plants by annual production, firm contribution, land, materials, and fuel rather than nameplate capacity alone.

title: Curtailment Is Endogenous
prompt: Add solar or wind to an actual grid in increments and show how marginal value and curtailment change as penetration rises.

title: Hydrogen Versus Direct Electrification
prompt: Start with the same amount of clean electricity and run it through batteries, hydrogen/reconversion, direct EV use, heat pumps, or synthetic fuels. Compare useful energy delivered.

title: The 2-BE Exercise
prompt: Take a reported well-water concentration such as 1 ppt. Calculate daily intake and place it beside relevant household exposures, occupational limits, reference doses, experimental doses, and effect levels on a logarithmic scale.

title: Detection Is Not Exposure Is Not Dose Is Not Harm
prompt: Pick one contaminant and place instrument detection limit, measured environmental concentration, typical intake, regulatory benchmark, occupational exposure, and toxicological effect level on one scale.

title: Make Parts per Trillion Physical
prompt: Make ppm, ppb, ppt, and ppq understandable, then translate the same concentration into a human dose under an explicit exposure route.

title: What Happens When Detection Improves 1,000x?
prompt: Hold the underlying environment unchanged while lowering the analytical detection limit. Show how the count of detected contaminants can change without exposure changing.

title: Hazard Classification Versus Actual Exposure
prompt: Pick a hazard classification and compare the doses or exposures underlying the hazard evidence with ordinary population exposures.

title: Linear-No-Threshold Surgery
prompt: Take the same low-dose exposure and estimate population risk using LNT, a threshold model, and another plausible dose-response form. Show how extrapolation changes the result.

title: Tiny Risk Times Huge Population
prompt: Apply several modeled individual risks to a large population, then show how expected cases depend on the assumed dose-response relationship and baseline risk.

title: Chemical Substitution
prompt: Pick a restricted chemical and a replacement. Compare exposure, toxicity, persistence, performance, cost, and new risks introduced by substitution.

title: Air-Pollution Mortality Model Surgery
prompt: Hold PM2.5 concentrations fixed and run multiple published concentration-response functions. Show how many estimated deaths come from model choice rather than a change in air.

title: Wildfire Smoke in Scale
prompt: Compare a severe smoke episode with annual urban exposure and other relevant exposure scales while keeping substance, route, duration, and uncertainty explicit.

title: Risk-Risk Tradeoff
prompt: Take a regulation that lowers one environmental exposure but changes another risk or resource use. Quantify both sides as far as the evidence permits.

title: Lithium Future Under Alternative Battery Chemistries
prompt: Take a published EV adoption path and calculate lithium demand under alternative battery chemistries, energy density, recycling, and average battery size.

title: The Copper Bottleneck
prompt: Build future copper demand from EVs, grids, renewables, buildings, and ordinary development under several transition pathways and compare with supply expansion and recycling.

title: Years of Reserves Remaining Is a Model
prompt: Calculate a conventional reserves-to-production ratio, then allow price, exploration, technology, recycling, and resource conversion to respond. Show how the depletion clock changes.

title: Geology Versus Supply Chain
prompt: For lithium or rare earths, map resources, mining, processing, refining, and manufacturing separately, then model the loss of one major processing country.

title: How Many New Mines?
prompt: Take a decarbonization scenario and estimate how many new mines of roughly today's typical size would be needed, then alter recycling, material intensity, and technology assumptions.

title: The Value of Substitution
prompt: Impose a large price increase on one critical mineral and identify technologically plausible substitution responses. Recalculate required quantities instead of holding engineering coefficients fixed.

title: Deep-Sea Versus Terrestrial Mining
prompt: For an equivalent quantity of a target metal, assemble comparable estimates of habitat disturbance, energy, waste, biodiversity uncertainty, and scale.

title: Land Spared by Yield
prompt: Take current production of several major crops and calculate the land required if yields were 10%, 25%, 50%, or 75% lower. Put the counterfactual land area on maps.

title: No Synthetic Nitrogen
prompt: Use agronomic literature to establish a defensible range of yield effects from eliminating synthetic nitrogen, then calculate additional cropland required to preserve current output.

title: Organic Yield-Gap Land Model
prompt: Take meta-analysis yield gaps by crop and calculate land required to maintain current output under partial or full conversion, allowing diet and waste assumptions to vary.

title: Yield Versus Biodiversity
prompt: Compare two futures producing identical food: high-yield farming on less land versus lower-intensity farming on more land. Use published species/land-use relationships and show the tradeoff.

title: Beef Land-Use Counterfactual
prompt: Remove 10%, 25%, 50%, or 100% of beef consumption and model pasture, feed crops, substitute foods, protein/calories, and emissions rather than simply deleting cattle.

title: Local-Food System Surgery
prompt: Reconstruct one meal's lifecycle footprint, then make the ingredients local while allowing seasonality, greenhouse heating, transport mode, storage, and production technique to change.

title: Food Miles With Transport Modes
prompt: Hold the food constant and move it by small truck, semi, rail, ship, or air. Show why distance alone is not the environmental variable.

title: Precision Agriculture
prompt: Take a heterogeneous field and compare uniform fertilizer application with sensor-guided variable-rate application under different accuracy assumptions.

title: GMO Farming-System Counterfactual
prompt: Pick one GM trait and reconstruct the farming system with versus without it: yield, pesticide use, tillage, fuel, land use, and substitute controls.

title: How Much Landfill Would We Actually Need?
prompt: Take current municipal waste, realistic compaction densities, and landfill depths. Calculate 10, 50, and 100 years of physical land area, then vary recycling, composting, and waste growth.

title: Landfill Harm Model
prompt: For one ton of mixed municipal waste, trace methane, leachate, transport, land use, and post-closure monitoring. Change methane capture and show how the climate result changes.

title: Recycling Where It Matters
prompt: Compare virgin-production and recycling energy for aluminum, glass, steel, paper, and PET, then impose the same recycling budget and ask which tons yield the most environmental gain.

title: Plastic Substitution
prompt: Replace one plastic package with glass, aluminum, paper, or reusable alternatives while holding service constant. Vary reuse, transport, washing, breakage, and recycling to find break-even conditions.

title: Western Water Reallocation
prompt: Take a fixed quantity of water in a low-value use and reallocate portions to municipal, environmental, or higher-value agricultural uses while tracking output, return flows, and third-party effects.

title: Water-Efficiency Paradox
prompt: Introduce more efficient irrigation. First assume conserved withdrawals become available to others; then allow acreage or crop choice to respond. Show why engineering and basin savings differ.

title: Desalination Future
prompt: Build the cost of supplying a coastal city with desalinated water under several electricity prices, utilization rates, brine costs, and financing assumptions.

title: Catch Shares Versus Race-to-Fish
prompt: Use a fishery model or dataset to compare open access, seasonal quotas, and individual tradable quotas while holding biological stock dynamics constant. Show effort, season length, catch, safety, and rents.

title: Endangered-Species Incentives
prompt: Construct a landowner payoff under no regulation, strict habitat restrictions, safe-harbor agreements, conservation payments, and tradable habitat credits.

title: Carbon-Tax Equivalence
prompt: Pick an emissions target. Calculate a carbon price that achieves it in a simplified model, then compare with a technology standard or subsidy that reaches the same environmental endpoint.

title: What Does $100 per Ton of CO2 Mean in Actual Life?
prompt: Translate a carbon price through gasoline, natural gas, electricity by generator type, cement, steel, airfare, and household spending, then change how revenue is returned.

title: Policy Cost per Ton
prompt: Pick several contemporary decarbonization policies and reproduce comparable cost-per-ton estimates, then change one central assumption in each and see how the comparison moves.

title: Carbon Offsets: Make Additionality Visible
prompt: Construct a project under worlds with and without the offset payment. Change baseline assumptions, leakage, permanence, and discounting and show how many credited tons survive.

title: 30x30 Is Not One Conservation Plan
prompt: Map what reaching a 30x30 target would mean under alternative selection rules such as cheapest land, highest biodiversity, highest carbon, connectivity, or geographic representation.

title: Wildfire Policy Counterfactual
prompt: Take one landscape and compare suppression-only, prescribed burning, thinning, home hardening, and combinations using the best available risk data or models.

title: Precautionary Policy Surgery
prompt: Take one contemporary environmental uncertainty and construct three strategies: immediate maximum action, wait for information, and adaptive policy that tightens as evidence arrives. Model both environmental loss and the cost of being wrong in the other direction.
